hook.line: Altamira is offering a bigger place in Chapinero, and Tomás and Vale are weighing it up on a napkin. To say two things come out even, you need one word that bends to fit the thing you are counting.
hook.es: Pero en Chapinero no hay tanta gente como aquí.
hook.en: But in Chapinero there aren't as many people as here.

examples.en: I work as much as you do.

examples.es: No hay tantos clientes como antes.
examples.en: There aren't as many customers as before.

examples.es: El apartamento nuevo tiene tanta luz como este.
examples.en: The new flat has as much light as this one.
Do you have as many things as I do?

examples.es: Vale no duerme tanto como Tomás.
examples.en: Vale doesn't sleep as much as Tomás.

examples.es: En Chapinero hay tanto ruido como aquí.
examples.en: In Chapinero there's as much noise as here.

examples.es: Los dos barrios son igual de tranquilos.
examples.en: The two neighbourhoods are equally quiet.

rule:
You already know *tan alto como*: as tall as. For as much and as many, Spanish uses *tanto*, and English's two words become one.

Before a thing, *tanto* matches that thing, just like *mucho*:
*tanto ruido*, *tanta gente*, *tantos clientes*, *tantas cosas*.
Then *como*, and the other side: *tanta luz como este*.

After a verb, it's simply *tanto como*, and it never changes: *trabajo tanto como tú*.

When there's nothing to compare against, *igual de* plus a describing word says just as: *es igual de caro*. Add *que* if you name the other side: *igual de ruidoso que el otro*.

As with *más que yo*, the other side uses *yo* and *tú*: *tanto como yo*.
smallPrint: Teachers call these comparisons of equality. *Tanto* with a thing is the agreeing kind; *tanto* after a verb is the fixed kind.

options: I work more than you.
I work as much as you do.
You work as much as I do.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick and type the whole sentence: *No hay ___ gente como antes.* (*tanto* or *tanta*) There aren't as many people as before.
yourTurn.answer: No hay tanta gente como antes.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick and type the whole sentence: *Vale trabaja ___ como tú.* (*tanto* or *tanta*) Vale works as much as you do.
yourTurn.why: It follows a verb, so it's always *tanto*.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick and type the whole sentence: *Hay ___ carros como ayer.* (*tantos* or *tanto*) There are as many cars as yesterday.
yourTurn.why: *Carros* is masculine and more than one, so *tantos*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: I don't have as much time as before.
yourTurn.answer: No tengo tanto tiempo como antes.
yourTurn.why: *Tiempo* is masculine and singular, so *tanto*, then *como antes*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: Don Hernando drinks as much coffee (*tinto*) as I do.
yourTurn.answer: Don Hernando toma tanto tinto como yo.
yourTurn.why: *Tanto* matches *tinto*, and the other side is *yo*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: Nobody cooks as much as Vale.
yourTurn.why: It comes after the verb *cocina*, so plain *tanto como*.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it equal: *En Chapinero hay más ruido que aquí.*
yourTurn.answer: En Chapinero hay tanto ruido como aquí.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: The flat in Chapinero is just as big. (Don't name what it's compared with.)
yourTurn.answer: El apartamento de Chapinero es igual de grande.
yourTurn.why: *Igual de* plus a describing word means just as, and it doesn't need a *como*.

pitfalls.wrong: No hay tan gente como antes.
pitfalls.right: No hay tanta gente como antes.
pitfalls.why: Almost. *Gente* is a thing, so you need *tanta*; *tan* only goes with describing words.

pitfalls.wrong: No hay tanto clientes como antes.
pitfalls.right: No hay tantos clientes como antes.
pitfalls.why: Before a thing, *tanto* matches it: *clientes* is plural, so *tantos*.
Close. *Tanto* pairs with *como*; *que* goes with *más* and *menos*.
After a verb there's no thing to match, so it stays *tanto*.

personal: Compare yourself with someone you know. Write one line with *tanto como* after a verb and one with *tanto*, *tanta*, *tantos* or *tantas* before a thing.
